attempts.note: Attempt 4's walk-fast champion meets the goal (about 276 on the held-out tracks, no falls, feet sharing the lead), but it spends about 99 points on motor effort per run against the skipper's 75, and its search is converging (σ 0.015). The champion is still chosen by the real score plus the gait tax.

attempts.title: Attempt 6: a wider network (64 hidden units), widened without forgetting
attempts.note: The shared leg controller has 32 hidden neurons. More capacity may allow a smoother, cheaper gait. The champion of attempt 4 is widened to 64 hidden neurons Net2Net-style: the new neurons start with zero outgoing weights, so the widened network walks exactly like the original (same 272.79 on the replay track, 1,859 parameters instead of 931), and CMA-ES then learns to use the extra capacity. Only the size changes (no extra effort weight), so it can be compared cleanly with attempt 5. Queued to start when attempt 4's last stage ends.

journal.title: Cheaper steps are winning: 279 with no falls
journal.text: Attempt 4's walk-fast stage stopped on a plateau at 17:28, and attempt 6 (the widened network) started automatically. On the goal check's twenty independent tracks, the current champions compare like this. Attempt 5, where effort counts one and a half times in training: 279.4 points, no falls, 117 front-foot changes per run, effort 84, finishing in about 991 steps. Attempt 4's final walker: 260.8 with 2 falls; it finishes faster, in 954 steps, but takes more risks. Attempt 6, 64 neurons, still early at generation 59: 260.3 with 2 falls. All three meet the goal, and all of them have cut effort from about 99 to about 84. The extra effort cost looks like the most useful change so far. Both runs keep training; if attempt 5 keeps its lead, the next experiment will combine it with the wider network.

journal.title: Model changes allowed: a wider network is queued (attempt 6)
journal.text: You gave me freedom to change the model itself. The first change: more capacity. The shared leg controller has only 32 hidden neurons. Attempt 6 widens the current champion to 64 using the Net2Net trick: the new neurons start with zero outgoing weights, so the wider network walks exactly like the original (checked: same 272.79 on the replay track), and evolution then learns how to use the extra neurons. Only the size changes, so it can be compared fairly with attempt 5 (extra effort cost). It starts automatically when attempt 4's walk-fast stage ends. Other model changes I can try next: two hidden layers, a memory (recurrent) layer, or repeating each action for two steps.

journal.title: Check-in: both runs progressing, nothing changed
journal.text: Attempt 4's walk-fast champion holds at 275.8 on the held-out tracks with no falls and the feet sharing the lead (foot 2 in front 54% of the time); it gained 7.4 points over the last 200 generations, just above the plateau threshold of 5, and its step size keeps shrinking (σ 0.012). Attempt 5 (effort counts 1.5 times) started eight minutes ago and is still at generation 8, so it's too early to judge. No changes, no new podcast episode yet.

journal.title: Still improving: attempt 5 polishes the walker
journal.text: The walk-fast stage of attempt 4 keeps improving, but slowly: its held-out champion went from 267 to 276 over about an hour, with no falls and the feet sharing the lead about fifty-fifty, while its search is narrowing (σ 0.015). The plateau rule will probably end it soon. Its main weakness is effort: about 99 points of motor effort per run, against 75 for the old skipper, which is why the skipper still scores about ten points more. Attempt 5 starts from this champion and makes effort count one and a half times in training, with the real fall cost and the same gait tax, a smaller step size and a larger population for fine-tuning. Both run side by side.

journal.title: GOAL MET: training wheels taught it to walk with alternating feet
journal.text: Attempt 4 worked. The support stages passed one after another, each in about an hour: support 2 after 68 generations, support 1 after 62, support 0.5 after 58. Then the real test, no support at all, passed at 14:15: on twenty held-out tracks, no falls, it reached the finish every time, 128 front-foot changes per run, and foot 2 led only a little over half the time. The goal check, on twenty different tracks, passes on every requirement for both the walk champion (257.5) and the walk-fast champion (264.1). On a hundred unseen tracks the walk-fast champion scores 263.9 with a spread of only ±1.1, no falls, and finishes all hundred in about 22 seconds each. Compared with the old skipping walker on the same hundred tracks: about 124 front-foot changes per run against almost none, 2 falls against 7, but about 10 points lower (260 vs 270), because alternating steps cost more motor effort. The walk-fast stage keeps training to make it faster and cheaper.

journal.title: Attempts 2 and 3 stuck on opposite sides; attempt 4 adds training wheels
journal.text: Attempt 2's stepping stage chose to stand still with its feet together: about one front-foot change per episode, because a step that falls costs more than standing earns. Attempt 3 did the opposite: it kept the alternating stumble, with about seventeen front-foot changes, but fell on all twenty test tracks at x ≈ 17, through both the step and the walk stage. Both were stopped. Attempt 4 uses training wheels: an upright torque on the body that keeps it from tipping, faded out over four stages (support 2, 1, 0.5, then none), followed by walking fast in the real game. With support 2 the stumbler never falls. Eighteen generations in, the best candidate already makes about eighty real crossing steps in an episode, foot 2 leads about 59% of the time, and it walks forward. The real test is whether the gait survives as the support is removed.

journal.title: Attempt 1 stopped; attempt 3 starts stepping from the stumbler
journal.text: Attempt 1's stepping stage never stopped tapping: for over 200 generations it made zero front-foot changes, with its feet split almost one unit apart, and its search had stopped exploring, so I stopped it at generation 454. I also found that the plateau watcher had quit at 08:29 because it didn't know about the curriculum scripts; it's fixed and running again. Attempt 2 is still in its balance stage: no falls, body level, but the feet are 0.53 units apart and the pass test wants under 0.4. With the freed cores, attempt 3 skips balance and starts the real-steps stage from v5-fresh, the one walker that already swaps its feet about 17 times per episode. It only has to learn not to fall while stepping.

journal.title: Attempt 1 found a shortcut: tapping in a split stance. Attempt 2 started.
journal.text: Stage 1 of attempt 1 passed, but its champion balances with its feet 2.9 units apart, foot 2 always in front: the skipper's stance. Stage 2 then learned to tap its feet alternately in that stance: about 70 alternating touchdowns per episode and zero front-foot changes, so the feet never pass each other, and the search has stopped exploring (σ 0.013). Attempt 2 fixes both: stage 1 now also pays for keeping the feet together, and stage 2 only counts a touchdown as a step when the foot coming down is the front foot and the legs alternate. Under the new step reward the tapper drops from 105 to 47 points while a real stepper can earn about 300. Attempt 1 keeps running as the baseline.

journal.title: v7-alt stopped; the curriculum gets the whole machine
journal.text: v7-alt (warm start from the alternating stumbler, with the per-distance gait tax) kept alternating, with foot 2 leading about 52% of the time and roughly 15 front-foot changes per episode, but after 177 generations every training episode still ended in a fall around x = 14. It is kept below as a comparison but no longer trains, so the curriculum runs alone on the four cores. The local dashboard on port 8771 now follows whichever curriculum stage is active.

journal.title: Curriculum started
journal.text: Every earlier attempt at proper walking had to find balance, alternating steps and forward progress at once, and settled for a shortcut each time: skipping with one leg as a prop (v3, v4, v5-warm), stumbling forward with alternating steps and falling (v5-fresh), or standing still (v6). The curriculum gives each skill its own training reward: 1 balance, 2 step (alternating feet, even in place), 3 walk, 4 walk fast. Each stage starts from the previous stage's champion. Attempt 1 started Wednesday 08:15. Running alongside for comparison: v7-alt, which starts from the alternating stumbler and has to learn balance while walking.
